title: Physics: Model Question Sets and Predicted Questions

toc.title: 4.1 Pattern and weight analysis of the Grade 11 Physics paper

html:
This chapter does three things. It reads the shape of the Grade 11 Physics paper (3 hours, full marks 75, Group A 11\times1, Group B 8\times5, Group C 3\times8) and shows how the 128 teaching hours are spread over the 26 units. It then sets two complete model papers to that grid, each fully solved. Finally it lists twenty-four predicted questions in ranked order, each with the reason it is predicted and a short model answer.

What "model" and "predicted" mean here

The model papers are original practice papers built to the CDC pattern; they are not NEB papers and are not claimed to resemble any particular year. A prediction is a judgement, not a leak: nobody outside the board knows the paper. The ranking uses three public things only — the teaching hours of each unit, how standard the question is (a derivation or definition every textbook treats), and whether it is a recurring numerical type. Treat the list as a revision order. No question in this chapter carries a past-paper year, because Grade 11 papers are not published by NEB.

4.1 Pattern and weight analysis of the Grade 11 Physics paper

4.1.1 The grid

Part Questions Marks What to expect
Group A 11 multiple-choice 11\times1 = 11 one mark each; drawn from the whole syllabus
Group B 8 short answer 8\times5 = 40 a mix of definition, short derivation and numerical
Group C 3 long answer 3\times8 = 24 derivation plus numerical, often in parts such as [3+3+2]

All questions are compulsory. Time per mark is 180/75 = 2.4 minutes: about 12 minutes for each Group B question and 19 for each Group C question.

4.1.2 Where the syllabus hours sit

Area Units Hours Share Expected presence in the paper
Mechanics 1–8 45 35 % the largest block: a Group C question and three or four Group B questions
Heat and Thermodynamics 9–13 26 20 % two Group B questions, sometimes a Group C part
Waves and Optics 14–18 15 12 % one or two Group B questions; mirror, lens or prism numerical
Electricity and Magnetism 19–23 27 21 % two Group B questions and often a Group C question
Modern Physics 24–26 15 12 % one Group B question; Group A items

4.1.3 Unit by unit: hours and the form the question usually takes

Unit Hours Typical form Priority
1 Physical quantities 3 dimensional analysis, significant figures medium
2 Vectors 4 resultant, resolution, dot and cross product high
3 Kinematics 5 equations of motion, projectile, relative velocity very high
4 Dynamics 6 momentum, impulse, friction, torque and equilibrium very high
5 Work, energy, power 6 work–energy theorem, collisions, conservation very high
6 Circular motion 6 centripetal force, conical pendulum, vertical circle, banking high
7 Gravitation 10 g variation, satellites, escape velocity very high
8 Elasticity 5 Young modulus, Hooke's law, elastic energy high
9 Heat and temperature 3 zeroth law, thermometry low
10 Thermal expansion 4 \alpha,\beta,\gamma relations, Dulong and Petit medium
11 Quantity of heat 6 calorimetry, latent heat, Newton's cooling high
12 Rate of heat flow 5 conductivity, Stefan–Boltzmann medium
13 Ideal gas 8 gas laws, kinetic theory, rms speed high
14 Curved mirrors 2 mirror formula, image numerical medium
15 Refraction at plane surfaces 4 apparent depth, critical angle high
16 Prisms 3 n formula, minimum deviation high
17 Lenses 3 lens formula, power, combination medium
18 Dispersion 3 dispersive power, spectrum medium
19 Electric charges 3 Coulomb's law, conservation medium
20 Electric field 3 field of point charge, field lines medium
21 Potential 4 potential, potential energy medium
22 Capacitor 7 combinations, energy, parallel plate very high
23 DC circuits 10 Kirchhoff, internal resistance, bridge very high
24 Nuclear physics 6 decay law, binding energy high
25 Solids 3 band theory, semiconductors medium
26 Recent trends 6 applications, descriptive medium

Two points follow. Nothing is safe to skip: Group A is spread over all 26 units. And the heavy units are the safest investment: Mechanics (45 h), Electricity (27 h) and Heat (26 h) together make up three-quarters of the teaching time.

4.2 Model Set 1

Time: 3 hours. Full marks: 75. Attempt all the questions. Figures in the margin indicate full marks. Use g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2} unless stated. This is an original practice paper, built to the CDC pattern.

Group A — Rewrite the correct option of each question in your answer sheet. (11\times1 = 11)

  1. The dimensions of impulse are [1]a[MLT^{-2}]b[MLT^{-1}]c[ML^{2}T^{-2}]d[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]
  2. A car starts from rest and reaches 20\ \text{m s}^{-1} in 5\ \text{s} with uniform acceleration. The distance covered is [1]a20\ \text{m}b50\ \text{m}c100\ \text{m}d200\ \text{m}
  3. A body of mass 2\ \text{kg} has kinetic energy 100\ \text{J}. Its speed is [1]a5\ \text{m s}^{-1}b7\ \text{m s}^{-1}c10\ \text{m s}^{-1}d50\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  4. At a depth equal to half the Earth's radius, the acceleration due to gravity is (g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2} at the surface) [1]a2.45\ \text{m s}^{-2}b4.9\ \text{m s}^{-2}c9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}d19.6\ \text{m s}^{-2}
  5. A spring of force constant 200\ \text{N m}^{-1} is stretched by 0.10\ \text{m}. The energy stored is [1]a0.5\ \text{J}b1.0\ \text{J}c2.0\ \text{J}d10\ \text{J}
  6. A 1\ \text{m} metal rod (\alpha = 1.2\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}) is heated through 100\ \text{K}. Its increase in length is [1]a0.12\ \text{mm}b1.2\ \text{mm}c12\ \text{mm}d120\ \text{mm}
  7. An object is placed 40\ \text{cm} from a concave mirror of focal length 20\ \text{cm}. The image distance is [1]a20\ \text{cm}b40\ \text{cm}c60\ \text{cm}d80\ \text{cm}
  8. The critical angle for a medium of refractive index 2 with respect to air is [1]a30^{\circ}b45^{\circ}c60^{\circ}d90^{\circ}
  9. The equivalent resistance of 6\ \Omega and 3\ \Omega in parallel is [1]a1\ \Omegab2\ \Omegac4.5\ \Omegad9\ \Omega
  10. The charge on a 5\ \mu\text{F} capacitor at 20\ \text{V} is [1]a4\ \mu\text{C}b25\ \mu\text{C}c100\ \mu\text{C}d400\ \mu\text{C}
  11. A radioactive sample has a half-life of 10 minutes. The fraction left after 30 minutes is [1]a1/2b1/4c1/8d1/16

Group B — Short answer questions. (8\times5 = 40)

  1. A stone is thrown horizontally at 15\ \text{m s}^{-1} from the top of a 80\ \text{m} cliff. Find the time to reach the ground, the horizontal distance covered, and the speed at impact. [5]
  2. State Newton's second law in terms of momentum. A 0.2\ \text{kg} ball hits a wall at 20\ \text{m s}^{-1} and rebounds at 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}; the contact lasts 0.01\ \text{s}. Find the impulse and the average force. [5]
  3. A uniform plank of weight 200\ \text{N} and length 4\ \text{m} rests on supports at its two ends. A person of weight 100\ \text{N} stands 1\ \text{m} from the left end. Find the reactions at the supports. [5]
  4. Define work done by a variable force. A force F = (3x + 2)\ \text{N} acts on a body as it moves from x = 0 to x = 4\ \text{m}. Find the work done. [5]
  5. Define specific latent heat of vaporization. How much heat is released when 200\ \text{g} of steam at 100^{\circ}\text{C} condenses and the water cools to 50^{\circ}\text{C}? (L_v = 2.26\times10^{6}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}, c_w = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}) [5]
  6. An object is 15\ \text{cm} from a concave lens of focal length 10\ \text{cm}. Find the position and magnification of the image and describe it. [5]
  7. Capacitors of 4\ \mu\text{F} and 8\ \mu\text{F} are connected in series across a 12\ \text{V} battery. Find the equivalent capacitance, the charge and the p.d. across each. [5]
  8. State Einstein's mass–energy relation. Find the energy equivalent to 1\ \text{g} of matter (c = 3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}) and explain what mass defect means. [5]

Group C — Long answer questions. (3\times8 = 24)

  1. (a) State the law of conservation of linear momentum and derive it from Newton's laws. [3](b) A 2\ \text{kg} body moving at 6\ \text{m s}^{-1} collides elastically head-on with a 4\ \text{kg} body at rest. Find the velocities after collision and verify that kinetic energy is conserved. [5] [8]
  2. (a) Derive an expression for the period of a conical pendulum. [4](b) A bob of mass 0.5\ \text{kg} on a string 1.0\ \text{m} long moves in a horizontal circle with the string at 60^{\circ} to the vertical. Find the period [2] and the tension. [2] [8]
  3. (a) Define e.m.f. and internal resistance and show that I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}. [3](b) Three cells, each of e.m.f. 1.5\ \text{V} and internal resistance 0.5\ \Omega, are joined in series to a 3.0\ \Omega resistor. Find the current and the terminal p.d. [3](c) Find the power in the resistor and the efficiency of the circuit. [2] [8]

4.2.1 Solutions to Model Set 1

Solutions — Group A

1. (b) — impulse = F\Delta t = change of momentum, [MLT^{-1}].

2. (b) — a = 20/5 = 4; s = \tfrac12at^{2} = \tfrac12(4)(25) = 50\ \text{m}.

3. (c) — v = \sqrt{2K/m} = \sqrt{200/2} = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}.

4. (b) — g_d = g(1 - d/R) = 9.8\times\tfrac12 = 4.9.

5. (b) — U = \tfrac12kx^{2} = \tfrac12(200)(0.01) = 1.0\ \text{J}.

6. (b) — \Delta l = l\alpha\Delta\theta = 1\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times100 = 1.2\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}.

7. (b) — the object is at C (u = 2f = 40), so the image is also at C: v = 40\ \text{cm}.

8. (a) — \sin C = 1/2, so C = 30^{\circ}.

9. (b) — \dfrac{6\times3}{6+3} = 2\ \Omega.

10. (c) — Q = CV = 5\times20 = 100\ \mu\text{C}.

11. (c) — three half-lives: (\tfrac12)^{3} = 1/8.

Solutions — Group B (12–19)

12. Vertical fall: h = \tfrac12gt^{2}, so t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times80}{10}} = 4\ \text{s}. Horizontal distance = 15\times4 = 60\ \text{m}. At impact v_y = gt = 40\ \text{m s}^{-1}, v_x = 15; speed = \sqrt{15^{2} + 40^{2}} = \sqrt{1825} = 42.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}.

13. The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force: F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}. Taking the rebound direction as positive, \Delta p = 0.2\,[15 - (-20)] = 7.0\ \text{N s} (impulse). F = \dfrac{7.0}{0.01} = 700\ \text{N}.

14. Let R_1 and R_2 be the reactions at the left and right ends. Moments about the right end: R_1(4) = 200(2) + 100(3) = 700, so R_1 = 175\ \text{N}. Vertical balance: R_1 + R_2 = 300, so R_2 = 125\ \text{N}.

15. For a variable force the work is the area under the F–x graph, W = \int F\,dx. W = \int_0^4(3x + 2)\,dx = \left[\tfrac32x^{2} + 2x\right]_0^4 = 24 + 8 = 32\ \text{J}.

16. The specific latent heat of vaporization is the heat needed to change 1\ \text{kg} of a liquid to vapour at its boiling point without change in temperature. Heat released = mL_v + mc\Delta\theta = 0.2(2.26\times10^{6}) + 0.2(4200)(50) = 4.52\times10^{5} + 4.2\times10^{4} = 4.94\times10^{5}\ \text{J}.

17. \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{5}{30}, so v = -6\ \text{cm} (virtual, on the same side as the object). m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{6}{15} = 0.4: erect, diminished, virtual.

18. C = \dfrac{4\times8}{4 + 8} = 2.67\ \mu\text{F}. In series each carries the same charge: Q = CV = 2.67\times12 = 32\ \mu\text{C}. V_1 = \dfrac{32}{4} = 8\ \text{V}; V_2 = \dfrac{32}{8} = 4\ \text{V} (sum 12\ \text{V} ✓).

19. E = mc^{2}: energy and mass are equivalent. E = 10^{-3}\times(3\times10^{8})^{2} = 9\times10^{13}\ \text{J}. Mass defect is the difference between the sum of the masses of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus; it appears as the binding energy \Delta m\,c^{2}.

Solutions — Group C (20–22)

20. (a) The total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant. For two bodies in collision, by Newton's third law F_{12} = -F_{21} for the same contact time \Delta t, so F_{12}\Delta t = -F_{21}\Delta t, i.e. \Delta p_1 = -\Delta p_2 and \Delta(p_1 + p_2) = 0. (b) Momentum: 2(6) = 2v_1 + 4v_2, so v_1 + 2v_2 = 6. Elastic: relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation, 6 = v_2 - v_1. Adding: 3v_2 = 12, so v_2 = 4\ \text{m s}^{-1} and v_1 = -2\ \text{m s}^{-1} (the 2\ \text{kg} body rebounds). Kinetic energy before: \tfrac12(2)(36) = 36\ \text{J}. After: \tfrac12(2)(4) + \tfrac12(4)(16) = 4 + 32 = 36\ \text{J} ✓.

21. (a) (Diagram: bob of mass m on a string of length l at angle \theta to the vertical; tension T along the string; weight mg downward; circle of radius r = l\sin\theta.) Vertically: T\cos\theta = mg. Horizontally the component T\sin\theta provides the centripetal force: T\sin\theta = m\omega^{2}r = m\omega^{2}l\sin\theta, so T = m\omega^{2}l. Combining, \omega^{2} = \dfrac{g}{l\cos\theta} and the period T_p = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l\cos\theta}{g}}. (b) T_p = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{1.0\times0.5}{10}} = 2\pi\times0.2236 = 1.41\ \text{s}. Tension: T = \dfrac{mg}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{0.5\times10}{0.5} = 10\ \text{N}.

22. (a) E.m.f. is the work done by the source per unit charge in carrying it round the complete circuit (equal to the terminal p.d. on open circuit). Internal resistance r is the resistance of the electrolyte and plates inside the cell. In a circuit with external resistance R, E = IR + Ir, so I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}. (b) In series, E_{tot} = 4.5\ \text{V} and r_{tot} = 1.5\ \Omega. I = \dfrac{4.5}{3.0 + 1.5} = 1.0\ \text{A}. Terminal p.d. V = E - Ir = 4.5 - 1.5 = 3.0\ \text{V}. (c) P = I^{2}R = 1^{2}\times3.0 = 3.0\ \text{W}. Efficiency = \dfrac{V}{E} = \dfrac{3.0}{4.5} = 66.7\ \%.

4.3 Model Set 2

Time: 3 hours. Full marks: 75. Attempt all the questions. Use g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2} unless stated. This is an original practice paper, built to the CDC pattern.

Group A — Rewrite the correct option of each question in your answer sheet. (11\times1 = 11)

  1. The dimensions of angular momentum are [1]a[MLT^{-1}]b[ML^{2}T^{-2}]c[ML^{2}T^{-1}]d[MLT^{-2}]
  2. A stone falls freely from rest through 45\ \text{m}. The time taken is [1]a1.5\ \text{s}b2\ \text{s}c3\ \text{s}d4.5\ \text{s}
  3. The momentum of a 0.5\ \text{kg} ball moving at 4\ \text{m s}^{-1} is [1]a0.5\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}b2\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}c8\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}d20\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}
  4. The escape velocity from the Earth's surface is about [1]a7.9\ \text{km s}^{-1}b11.2\ \text{km s}^{-1}c15\ \text{km s}^{-1}d3\times10^{5}\ \text{km s}^{-1}
  5. A force of 10\ \text{N} acts at 60^{\circ} to the displacement of 5\ \text{m}. The work done is [1]a50\ \text{J}b25\ \text{J}c43.3\ \text{J}d0
  6. The heat needed to raise 2\ \text{kg} of water by 10\ \text{K} (c = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}) is [1]a8.4\times10^{3}\ \text{J}b4.2\times10^{4}\ \text{J}c8.4\times10^{4}\ \text{J}d8.4\times10^{5}\ \text{J}
  7. The speed of light in glass of refractive index 1.5 is [1]a1.5\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}b2.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}c3.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}d4.5\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  8. The power of a convex lens of focal length 50\ \text{cm} is [1]a0.5\ \text{D}b1\ \text{D}c2\ \text{D}d5\ \text{D}
  9. The field between two plates 2\ \text{cm} apart at a p.d. of 100\ \text{V} is [1]a50\ \text{V m}^{-1}b200\ \text{V m}^{-1}c5000\ \text{V m}^{-1}d20\,000\ \text{V m}^{-1}
  10. The heat produced by 2\ \text{A} in a 5\ \Omega resistor in 10\ \text{s} is [1]a100\ \text{J}b200\ \text{J}c400\ \text{J}d1000\ \text{J}
  11. After an \alpha-decay of ^{238}_{92}\text{U}, the mass number of the daughter nucleus is [1]a238b236c234d232

Group B — Short answer questions. (8\times5 = 40)

  1. Two blocks of 3\ \text{kg} and 2\ \text{kg} lie on a smooth table, connected by a light string. A horizontal force of 10\ \text{N} pulls the 3\ \text{kg} block. Find the acceleration and the tension in the string. [5]
  2. A 10\ \text{kg} block slides down a rough incline of 30^{\circ} with \mu_k = 0.2. Find its acceleration. [5]
  3. Derive an expression for the escape velocity and evaluate it for g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2} and R = 6.4\times10^{6}\ \text{m}. [5]
  4. A load of 50\ \text{N} is hung from a steel wire 2\ \text{m} long and 0.5\ \text{mm} in radius (Y = 2\times10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2}). Find the extension. [5]
  5. Define linear expansivity. A steel rail 12\ \text{m} long (\alpha = 1.2\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}) is laid at 10^{\circ}\text{C}. Find the gap needed between rails for a rise to 40^{\circ}\text{C}, and say why gaps are left. [5]
  6. An object is 30\ \text{cm} from a convex mirror of focal length 20\ \text{cm}. Find the image position and magnification. [5]
  7. Charges +4\ \mu\text{C} and -4\ \mu\text{C} are 10\ \text{cm} apart. Find the electric field and the potential at the midpoint. [5]
  8. Define activity of a radioactive source and state its SI unit. A source has an initial activity of 800\ \text{Bq} and half-life 2\ \text{h}; find its activity after 6\ \text{h}. Name one property that distinguishes \alpha from \gamma radiation. [5]

Group C — Long answer questions. (3\times8 = 24)

  1. (a) State and prove the work–energy theorem for a constant force. [3](b) A pump raises 900\ \text{kg} of water per minute through 20\ \text{m}. Find the output power, and the input power if the efficiency is 75\ \%. [3](c) Define power and state its SI unit. [2] [8]
  2. (a) Derive the minimum speeds at the top and at the bottom of a vertical circle for a body on a string. [5](b) For a 0.2\ \text{kg} body on a string of length 0.9\ \text{m}, find the minimum speeds at the top and bottom, and the tension at the bottom at that speed. [3] [8]
  3. (a) State the laws of refraction and derive n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}} for a nearly normal view. [4](b) A tank holds 12\ \text{cm} of water (n = 4/3) under 9\ \text{cm} of oil (n = 1.5). Find the apparent depth of the bottom as seen from above. [4] [8]

4.3.1 Solutions to Model Set 2

Solutions — Group A

1. (c) — L = mvr: [M][LT^{-1}][L] = [ML^{2}T^{-1}].

2. (c) — t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{90/10} = 3\ \text{s}.

3. (b) — p = mv = 0.5\times4 = 2.

4. (b) — v_e = \sqrt{2gR} \approx 11.2\ \text{km s}^{-1}; (a) is the orbital speed near the surface.

5. (b) — W = Fs\cos\theta = 10\times5\times0.5 = 25\ \text{J}.

6. (c) — Q = mc\Delta\theta = 2\times4200\times10 = 8.4\times10^{4}\ \text{J}.

7. (b) — v = c/n = 3\times10^{8}/1.5 = 2\times10^{8}.

8. (c) — P = 1/f = 1/0.5 = 2\ \text{D}.

9. (c) — E = V/d = 100/0.02 = 5000\ \text{V m}^{-1}.

10. (b) — I^{2}Rt = 4\times5\times10 = 200\ \text{J}.

11. (c) — \alpha-emission removes 4 from the mass number: 238 - 4 = 234.

Solutions — Group B (12–19)

12. Treat the two blocks as one system: a = \dfrac{F}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}. The string alone accelerates the 2\ \text{kg} block: T = m_2a = 2\times2 = 4\ \text{N}.

13. Down the incline: mg\sin\theta - \mu mg\cos\theta = ma, so a = g(\sin30^{\circ} - 0.2\cos30^{\circ}) = 10(0.5 - 0.1732) = 3.27\ \text{m s}^{-2}.

14. To escape, the kinetic energy given must equal the work against gravity to infinity: \tfrac12mv_e^{2} = \dfrac{GMm}{R}. With GM = gR^{2}: v_e = \sqrt{2gR}. v_e = \sqrt{2\times9.8\times6.4\times10^{6}} = \sqrt{1.254\times10^{8}} = 1.12\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1} = 11.2\ \text{km s}^{-1}.

15. A = \pi r^{2} = \pi(0.5\times10^{-3})^{2} = 7.85\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2}. \Delta l = \dfrac{FL}{AY} = \dfrac{50\times2}{7.85\times10^{-7}\times2\times10^{11}} = 6.4\times10^{-4}\ \text{m} = 0.64\ \text{mm}.

16. Linear expansivity is the fractional increase in length per unit original length per kelvin rise in temperature, \alpha = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l\Delta\theta}. \Delta l = 12\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times30 = 4.3\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 4.3\ \text{mm}. Gaps let the rails lengthen in summer; without them they would buckle.

17. With f = -20 and u = 30: \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{5}{60}, so v = -12\ \text{cm} (virtual, behind the mirror). m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{12}{30} = 0.4 (erect, diminished).

18. Each charge is 5\ \text{cm} from the midpoint. E_1 = \dfrac{kq}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times4\times10^{-6}}{(0.05)^{2}} = 1.44\times10^{7}\ \text{N C}^{-1}. Both fields point towards the negative charge, so they add: E = 2.88\times10^{7}\ \text{N C}^{-1}. Potential: V = k\left(\dfrac{4\times10^{-6}}{0.05} + \dfrac{-4\times10^{-6}}{0.05}\right) = 0.

19. Activity is the number of nuclei disintegrating per second; the SI unit is the becquerel (1\ \text{Bq} = 1 decay per second). 6\ \text{h} = 3 half-lives, so A = 800\times\tfrac18 = 100\ \text{Bq}. Distinction: \alpha particles are helium nuclei, strongly ionizing and stopped by paper; \gamma rays are electromagnetic waves, weakly ionizing and very penetrating.

Solutions — Group C (20–22)

20. (a) For a constant net force F, v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as and F = ma. Multiply by m/2: \tfrac12mv^{2} - \tfrac12mu^{2} = mas = Fs = W. The net work done equals the change in kinetic energy. (b) Output power = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = \dfrac{900\times10\times20}{60} = 3000\ \text{W}. Input = \dfrac{3000}{0.75} = 4000\ \text{W}. (c) Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t; the unit is the watt (\text{J s}^{-1}).

21. (a) (Diagram: circle of radius r with the body at the top and bottom, tension T towards the centre, weight mg downward.) At the top: T_t + mg = \dfrac{mv_t^{2}}{r}. The least speed is when T_t = 0: v_t = \sqrt{gr}. Between bottom and top the body rises 2r; energy conservation gives \tfrac12mv_b^{2} = \tfrac12mv_t^{2} + mg(2r), so v_b^{2} = gr + 4gr = 5gr and v_b = \sqrt{5gr}. At the bottom, T_b - mg = \dfrac{mv_b^{2}}{r} = 5mg, so T_b = 6mg. (b) v_t = \sqrt{10\times0.9} = 3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}; v_b = \sqrt{5\times10\times0.9} = \sqrt{45} = 6.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}. T_b = 6mg = 6\times0.2\times10 = 12\ \text{N}.

22. (a) Laws: the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal lie in one plane; \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} is constant for a given pair of media (Snell). (Diagram: object O at depth d in the denser medium; a ray OA at a small angle r to the normal refracts at A into air at angle i; the eye traces it back to the apparent position I at depth d'.) With x the horizontal distance of A from the normal, for small angles \sin r \approx \tan r = x/d and \sin i \approx \tan i = x/d'. Hence n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{x/d'}{x/d} = \dfrac{d}{d'}, i.e. n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}. (b) The apparent depth is the sum of the apparent thicknesses of each layer: \dfrac{9}{1.5} + \dfrac{12}{4/3} = 6 + 9 = 15\ \text{cm} (the real depth is 21\ \text{cm}).

4.4 Predicted Questions — ranked

The ranking is by teaching hours of the unit and how standard the question is. Each prediction states its reason. Tier A are the questions a paper on this syllabus almost has to contain in some form; Tier B are likely; Tier C are possible and worth a pass if time remains. These are judgements, never guarantees.

4.4.1 Tier A — revise first

P1. Equations of motion by the graphical method, and a numerical (unit 3, [5\text{ or }8]; Mechanics). Why: kinematics is the foundation of Mechanics (45 h), and the graphical derivation is named in the syllabus. Outline: v = u + at from the slope; s as the area under the v–t graph; v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as by eliminating t. Example: u = 5, a = 2, t = 6 gives v = 17\ \text{m s}^{-1}, s = 66\ \text{m}. P2. Projectile motion: time of flight, maximum height, range (unit 3, [5\text{ or }8]). Why: named in the syllabus and the standard application of vectors and kinematics. Outline: T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}, H = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{2g}, R = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin2\theta}{g}; maximum range at 45^{\circ}; R equal for \theta and 90^{\circ} - \theta. P3. Conservation of linear momentum, with an elastic or inelastic collision (unit 4/5, [5\text{ or }8]). Why: named in both units, and gives a clean numerical. Outline: proof from Newton's third law; elastic: v_1 = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}u, v_2 = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}u; inelastic: v = \dfrac{m_1u}{m_1 + m_2}, kinetic energy lost. P4. Laws of solid friction and angle of repose (unit 4, [5]). Why: the syllabus names the laws and their verification. Outline: four laws; \mu = \tan\theta at the angle of friction; incline with and without friction. P5. Work–energy theorem and conservation of energy (unit 5, [5\text{ or }8]). Why: a six-hour unit with a standard proof. Outline: W = \Delta K; K + U constant for a freely falling body; check at two heights. P6. Satellite: orbital speed, period, geostationary orbit (unit 7, [8]). Why: gravitation has the largest unit weight (10 h) and the satellite topics fill half the unit. Outline: v = \sqrt{GM/(R+h)}; T = 2\pi\sqrt{(R+h)^{3}/GM}; energy K = GMm/2r, U = -GMm/r, E = -GMm/2r; geostationary conditions. P7. Variation of g with altitude and depth; escape velocity (unit 7, [5]). Why: named in the syllabus; clean derivations. Outline: g_h = g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^{2}; g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right); v_e = \sqrt{2gR} = 11.2\ \text{km s}^{-1}. P8. Young modulus, stress, strain and elastic energy (unit 8, [5]). Why: a numerical type with exact formulae. Outline: Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\Delta l}; U = \tfrac12F\Delta l; energy per volume \tfrac12\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}. P9. Combination of capacitors and energy stored (unit 22, [5]). Why: a seven-hour unit with direct numericals. Outline: series \dfrac{1}{C} = \sum\dfrac{1}{C_i}; parallel C = \sum C_i; U = \tfrac12CV^{2}. P10. Kirchhoff's laws with a two-loop or bridge numerical; internal resistance (unit 23, [5\text{ or }8]). Why: DC circuits carry 10 hours, the joint-largest unit weight. Outline: \sum I = 0 and \sum E = \sum IR; I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}; Wheatstone balance \dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}. P11. Calorimetry and latent heat numerical (unit 11, [5]). Why: a recurring numerical type and a six-hour unit. Outline: heat lost = heat gained; list each stage: warm, melt, warm, boil. P12. Kinetic theory: P = \tfrac13\rho\overline{c^{2}} and rms speed (unit 13, [5\text{ or }8]). Why: the standard derivation of an eight-hour unit. Outline: momentum change 2mu_x; time 2l/u_x; \overline{u_x^{2}} = \tfrac13\overline{c^{2}}; c_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}.

4.4.2 Tier B — likely

P13. Conical pendulum and motion in a vertical circle (unit 6, [5\text{ or }8]). Why: named in the syllabus; clean derivations. Outline: T = 2\pi\sqrt{l\cos\theta/g}; v_{top} = \sqrt{gr}, v_{bottom} = \sqrt{5gr}, T_{bottom} = 6mg. P14. Banking of roads (unit 6, [5]). Why: named in the syllabus. Outline: \tan\theta = \dfrac{v^{2}}{rg}; with friction v^{2} = rg\,\dfrac{\mu + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu\tan\theta}. P15. Moment, torque and equilibrium of a beam (unit 4, [5]). Why: a standard numerical (two supports, a hanging load). Outline: take moments about one support; sum of forces zero. P16. Triangle, parallelogram law and resolution of vectors; scalar and vector products (unit 2, [5]). Why: four hours, all formulae exact. Outline: R = \sqrt{P^{2} + Q^{2} + 2PQ\cos\theta}; \tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}; \vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta, |\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\theta. P17. Thermal expansion: \gamma = 3\alpha and the apparent expansion of a liquid (unit 10, [5]). Why: named relations in the syllabus. Outline: \beta = 2\alpha, \gamma = 3\alpha; \gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_g. P18. Newton's law of cooling and Stefan–Boltzmann law (units 11/12, [5]). Why: named in the syllabus; formula-based. Outline: rate \propto excess temperature; P = \sigma AT^{4}; net loss \sigma A(T^{4} - T_0^{4}). P19. Refraction: apparent depth, critical angle, total internal reflection (unit 15, [5]). Why: four hours; standard numericals. Outline: n = \dfrac{\text{real}}{\text{apparent}}; \sin C = 1/n; optical fibre as application. P20. Prism: n in terms of A and D_m (unit 16, [5]). Why: the prism formula is the syllabus's single derivation of its unit. Outline: D = i_1 + i_2 - A; n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A + D_m}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}; thin prism D = (n - 1)A.

4.4.3 Tier C — possible

P21. Radioactive decay law and half-life (unit 24, [5]). Why: the one derivation of Modern Physics; a standard numerical. Outline: N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}; T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda. P22. Binding energy and mass defect (unit 24, [5]). Why: a numerical type with a fixed constant (1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}). Outline: B = \Delta m\times931.5\ \text{MeV}; binding energy per nucleon. P23. Band theory: conductor, semiconductor, insulator; n-type and p-type (unit 25, [5]). Why: the whole content of a three-hour unit. Outline: band diagrams; doping with Group V (donor) or Group III (acceptor) atoms. P24. Dispersive power and the pure spectrum (unit 18, [5]). Why: a standard definition with a one-line numerical. Outline: \omega = \dfrac{n_v - n_r}{n_y - 1}; the pure spectrum is formed with two prisms or a lens and a screen.

Chapter summary

  • The Physics paper is 75 marks: 11\times1, 8\times5 and 3\times8; Mechanics (45 h), Electricity (27 h) and Heat (26 h) make three-quarters of the teaching time.
  • Two complete model sets, built to the grid, are solved in full; each answer shows the law, the substitution with units and the final result.
  • Recurring numerical types: equations of motion and projectiles; collisions and impulse; g variation and satellites; Y = FL/A\Delta l; calorimetry; capacitor combinations; internal resistance and Kirchhoff; half-life.
  • The twenty-four predicted questions are ranked by unit hours and standardness; they are judgements, not leaks.
  • In the hall: formula first, then substitution with units, then the answer; draw the diagram before the algebra; convert to kelvin, metres and radians before calculating.

Practice questions

Group A — Multiple choice (1 mark each)

  1. The tension in a conical-pendulum string of mass m at angle \theta to the vertical is [1]amg\sin\thetabmg\cos\thetacmg/\cos\thetadmg/\sin\theta
  2. The maximum range of a projectile launched at 20\ \text{m s}^{-1} (g = 10) is [1]a20\ \text{m}b40\ \text{m}c80\ \text{m}d200\ \text{m}
  3. Two 6\ \mu\text{F} capacitors in parallel give [1]a3\ \mu\text{F}b6\ \mu\text{F}c12\ \mu\text{F}d36\ \mu\text{F}
  4. The minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle of radius 1.6\ \text{m} (g = 10) is [1]a2\ \text{m s}^{-1}b4\ \text{m s}^{-1}c8\ \text{m s}^{-1}d16\ \text{m s}^{-1}
Answers to Group A

1. (c) — T\cos\theta = mg.

2. (b) — R_{max} = u^{2}/g = 400/10 = 40\ \text{m}.

3. (c) — parallel capacitances add: 6 + 6 = 12.

4. (b) — \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{16} = 4\ \text{m s}^{-1}.

Group B — Short answer (5 marks each)

  1. A 60\ \text{kg} person stands on a lift accelerating upward at 2\ \text{m s}^{-2}. Find the apparent weight (g = 10). [5]
  2. Find the heat needed to raise 0.5\ \text{kg} of ice at 0^{\circ}\text{C} to water at 20^{\circ}\text{C} (L_f = 3.36\times10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}). [5]
  3. Find the equivalent resistance between the ends when 2\ \Omega is in series with the parallel pair 3\ \Omega and 6\ \Omega. [5]
  4. A sample has 5\ \text{g} left after 12 days from 40\ \text{g}. Find its half-life. [5]
Answers to Group B

1. R - mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 60\times12 = 720\ \text{N} (apparent weight, compared with 600\ \text{N} at rest).

2. Melting: 0.5\times3.36\times10^{5} = 1.68\times10^{5}\ \text{J}. Warming: 0.5\times4200\times20 = 4.2\times10^{4}\ \text{J}. Total 2.10\times10^{5}\ \text{J}.

3. Parallel: \dfrac{3\times6}{9} = 2\ \Omega; total 2 + 2 = 4\ \Omega.

4. 40/5 = 8 = 2^{3}, so 3T_{1/2} = 12 days and T_{1/2} = 4 days.

Group C — Long answer (8 marks each)

  1. Derive the expression for the energy stored in a charged capacitor and find the energy released when a 20\ \mu\text{F} capacitor charged to 50\ \text{V} is discharged. [8]
  2. Derive the relation between the focal length and radius of curvature of a concave mirror and find the image formed by an object 30\ \text{cm} from a concave mirror of f = 10\ \text{cm}. [8]
Answers to Group C

1. Charging from q to q + dq against the p.d. V = q/C needs dW = \dfrac{q}{C}\,dq. Total work W = \int_0^Q\dfrac{q}{C}\,dq = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \tfrac12CV^{2}, stored as electric field energy. U = \tfrac12(20\times10^{-6})(50)^{2} = 0.025\ \text{J}, which is released as heat or light on discharge.

2. A ray parallel to the axis strikes the mirror at D; the radius CD is the normal, so the angle of incidence and reflection are equal, \theta. The reflected ray cuts the axis at F. In \triangle CDF, \angle FCD = \angle CDF = \theta (since DA \parallel CP), so CF = FD; for a small aperture FD \approx FP, hence CP = CF + FP = 2FP and f = R/2. Numerical: \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{2}{30}, so v = 15\ \text{cm} (real, inverted); m = -\dfrac{15}{30} = -0.5 (diminished).
